questions.stem: Let $G$ be a weighted directed acyclic graph with $m$ edges and $n$ vertices. Given $G$ and a source vertex $s$ in $G$, which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from $s$ to all vertices that are reachable from $s$ in $G$?

steps.title: Definitions and the deciding rule
steps.body: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph with no cycle, so its vertices can be listed in a topological order: every edge goes from an earlier vertex to a later one. A shortest path from $s$ to $v$ is a path whose edge weights add up to the smallest total. Relaxing an edge $(u,v)$ means testing whether $d[u]+w(u,v)$ beats the current $d[v]$ and, if so, lowering $d[v]$. The rule that decides the question: if the edges out of each vertex are relaxed in topological order, every vertex already holds its final distance when its turn comes, so each edge needs exactly one relaxation. The sign of the weights does not matter.

steps.title: Cost of the two phases
steps.body: Phase 1 is a topological sort, by DFS or by repeatedly removing a vertex of in-degree 0. It touches every vertex and edge once: $\Theta(n+m)$. Phase 2 sets $d[s]=0$ and every other distance to $\infty$, walks the order and relaxes each outgoing edge once: another $\Theta(n+m)$. Reading the input already costs $\Omega(n+m)$, so nothing can beat this.

steps.title: Compare with the other options
steps.body: Dijkstra with a Fibonacci heap costs $\Theta(m+n\log n)$, option (B), and breaks on negative weights. Bellman-Ford costs $\Theta(nm)$, option (C). Floyd-Warshall costs $\Theta(n^3)$, option (D), and answers all pairs, which is more than asked. The fastest is $\Theta(m+n)$, option (A).

shortcut.body: Weighted DAG, one source: topological order, then one relaxation pass, $\Theta(n+m)$. The option with no log and no product wins.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(m+n\log n)$ because 'shortest path means Dijkstra'. That is the best general bound for non-negative weights; the acyclic structure removes the need for a priority queue.
Choosing $\Theta(nm)$ because weights might be negative. Bellman-Ford handles negatives on any graph, but a DAG's topological order does the same job in a single pass.
Choosing $\Theta(n^3)$ after thinking of Floyd-Warshall. That solves all pairs; the question wants one source.

recognize.clues: The graph is a weighted DAG with one source, and the question asks for the fastest worst-case algorithm. Acyclic plus single-source points to a topological order followed by one relaxation pass.
recognize.contrast: Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford are built for graphs that may have cycles, and Bellman-Ford copes with negative weights by repeating passes. A DAG gives the order for free, so neither is needed.

check.body: Test on a three-vertex DAG with edges $s\to a$ of weight 1, $a\to t$ of weight $-3$ and $s\to t$ of weight 0. The order $s,a,t$ gives $d[a]=1$ and then $d[t]=\min(0,-2)=-2$ after one relaxation per edge, three relaxations for $m=3$. Dijkstra would settle $t$ at 0 too early, which shows why the ordering pass is what makes a single sweep enough.

questions.stem:
Let $G(V,E)$ be an undirected, edge-weighted graph with integer weights. The weight of a path is the sum of the weights of the edges in that path. The length of a path is the number of edges in that path.

Let $s \in V$ be a vertex in $G$. For every $u \in V$ and for every $k \ge 0$, let $d_k(u)$ denote the weight of a shortest path (in terms of weight) from $s$ to $u$ of length at most $k$. If there is no path from $s$ to $u$ of length at most $k$, then $d_k(u)=\infty$.

Consider the statements:

S1: For every $k \ge 0$ and $u \in V$, $d_{k+1}(u) \le d_k(u)$.

S2: For every $(u,v) \in E$, if $(u,v)$ is part of a shortest path (in terms of weight) from $s$ to $v$, then for every $k \ge 0$, $d_k(u) \le d_k(v)$.

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
Neither S1 nor S2 is true

solutionDiagram.alt: Triangle s, u, v with weights 5, -4 and 10, and the table d1 and d2 showing d2(u) = 5 exceeds d2(v) = 1.

steps.title: What $d_k(u)$ means
steps.body: $d_k(u)$ is the best weight you can get to $u$ using at most $k$ edges. This is exactly the table that Bellman-Ford builds: after round $k$ it holds $d_k$. Two plain facts come with it. First, 'at most $k+1$ edges' includes every walk of 'at most $k$ edges', so the smaller set of choices cannot beat the larger one. Second, weights are integers and may be negative, so a cheap route can need many edges.

steps.title: Test S1
steps.body: The set of paths with at most $k+1$ edges contains the set with at most $k$ edges. A minimum over a larger set is never larger. So $d_{k+1}(u)\le d_k(u)$ for every $u$ and $k$, including the case $d_k(u)=\infty$. S1 is true.

steps.title: Test S2 with a counterexample
steps.body: S2 claims the earlier vertex of a shortest-path edge is never more expensive at any budget $k$. Try three vertices: $w(s,u)=5$, $w(u,v)=-4$, $w(s,v)=10$. The shortest path to $v$ is $s\to u\to v$ with weight $1$, so $(u,v)$ lies on it. With two edges allowed, $d_2(u)=5$ (a longer route to $u$ through $v$ costs $10-4=6$) while $d_2(v)=1$. Then $d_2(u)=5>1=d_2(v)$, so S2 fails. The negative edge makes the 'later' vertex cheaper. The answer is (A): only S1 is true.

shortcut.body: S1 is a min over a growing set, so true at once. For S2 try one small graph with a negative edge, or a mixed-budget case; a general 'monotone along a path' claim almost always breaks with negative weights.

traps.text: Choosing 'only S2' means believing the order along a shortest path holds at every budget. It holds for the final distances with non-negative weights, not for the bounded-length tables $d_k$ with negative weights.
Choosing 'both' trusts S2 because it sounds like the triangle inequality. A counterexample with $w(u,v)=-4$ breaks it at $k=2$.
Choosing 'neither' misreads S1 as strict. The statement uses $\le$, so the equal case is fine, and S1 is true.

recognize.clues: The quantity $d_k(u)$ is the best weight using at most $k$ edges, which is the table Bellman-Ford fills round by round. The integer weights, possibly negative, rule out a settled-by-weight view.
recognize.contrast: Dijkstra finalises vertices in order of weight, so one is tempted to think the earlier vertex of a shortest-path edge is always cheaper. With negative edges that order breaks, and Bellman-Ford counts edges, not weight order.

check.body: Recompute the S2 example by listing every walk of at most 2 edges from $s$. To $u$: $s\to u$ costs 5 and $s\to v\to u$ costs $10-4=6$, so $d_2(u)=5$. To $v$: $s\to v$ costs 10 and $s\to u\to v$ costs $5-4=1$, so $d_2(v)=1$. At $k=1$ the order is the other way, $d_1(u)=5<10=d_1(v)$, so the order of the two ends flips between $k=1$ and $k=2$, and S2 fails at $k=2$.

questions.stem:
Let $G(V,E)$ be a simple, undirected, edge-weighted graph with unique edge weights.

Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees (MST) of $G$ is/are true?
options: In every cycle $C$ of $G$, the edge with the largest weight in $C$ is not in any MST
In every cycle $C$ of $G$, the edge with the smallest weight in $C$ is in every MST
For every vertex $v \in V$, the edge with the largest weight incident on $v$ is not in any MST
For every vertex $v \in V$, the edge with the smallest weight incident on $v$ is in every MST

steps.title: The two rules behind every MST fact
steps.body: A spanning tree touches every vertex with no cycle. The cycle property: in any cycle, the heaviest edge is not needed, because removing it leaves the rest connected. The cut property: split the vertices into two groups; the lightest edge crossing the split belongs to every MST. Unique weights remove ties, so 'the heaviest' and 'the lightest' are single edges, and the two properties hold for every MST, not just some.

steps.title: Statements A and B (cycles)
steps.body: (A) In any cycle $C$ the heaviest edge is the strict maximum, so by the cycle property no MST uses it. True. (B) The lightest edge of a cycle is not protected, because the cut property guards an edge only when it is the lightest across some cut. Counterexample on vertices $a,b,c,d$ with $ac=1$, $cb=2$, $ab=5$, $bd=6$, $da=7$. In the cycle $a,b,d$ the lightest edge is $ab=5$. But $ab$ is the heaviest edge of the triangle $a,b,c$ ($1,2,5$), so the MST $\{ac,cb,bd\}$ of weight 9 leaves it out. B is false.

steps.title: Statements C and D (vertices)
steps.body: Take any vertex $v$ and the cut $\{v\}$ versus the rest. The lightest edge at $v$ crosses this cut, so by the cut property it is in every MST. (D) is true. The heaviest edge at $v$ is not excluded: if $v$ has only one edge, that edge is a bridge and must be in the tree, and even with several edges the heaviest one can be the only link to a part of the graph. So (C) is false. The true statements are A and D.

shortcut.body: Cycle property gives A, the cut around a single vertex gives D. Kill B and C with the smallest counterexamples: B with a lightest cycle edge that is the heaviest edge of another cycle, C with a degree-1 vertex.

traps.text: Statement B reads 'the lightest edge of any cycle is in every MST'. The cut property only protects an edge that is lightest across a cut; the lightest edge of one cycle can still be the heaviest edge of another cycle, which is the case the cycle property removes.

Statement C extends 'heaviest edge in a cycle is out' to 'heaviest edge at a vertex is out'. A pendant vertex has one edge, which is both its lightest and heaviest, and a bridge belongs to every spanning tree.

recognize.clues: The weights are unique, and each statement is about the largest or smallest edge in a cycle or at a vertex being in or out of every MST. That is the language of the cycle property and the cut property.
recognize.contrast: The lightest edge of a cycle is not protected by the cut property, since it need not be lightest across any cut; do not mix the two properties. Only the cycle property says anything about heaviest edges.

check.body: Test statement C on a triangle with weights 1, 2, 3 and a new vertex $v$ joined to one triangle vertex by an edge of weight 9. The heaviest edge at $v$ has weight 9, yet it is the only way to reach $v$, so every spanning tree contains it. Kruskal confirms: it takes 1 and 2, rejects 3 as a cycle edge, then must take 9. So a heaviest incident edge can be in the MST.

variation.stem: A graph on vertices $1,\dots,5$ has distinct edge weights: $w(1,2)=3$, $w(2,3)=1$, $w(1,3)=4$, $w(3,4)=2$, $w(4,5)=6$, $w(3,5)=5$, $w(2,4)=7$. Which of the following is/are true about its minimum spanning tree?
options: The edge $(1,3)$ is in the MST.
The edge $(3,5)$ is in the MST.
The total weight of the MST is 11.
The edge $(2,4)$ is in the MST.
variation.explanation: Kruskal takes weights 1, 2, 3 on edges $(2,3),(3,4),(1,2)$, rejects 4 because $(1,3)$ closes a cycle, takes 5 on $(3,5)$, and then has 4 edges. The weight is $1+2+3+5=11$, so B and C are true. Edges $(1,3)$ and $(2,4)$ are the heaviest edges of cycles, so A and D fail.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pseudocode for depth-first search (DFS) algorithm which takes a directed graph $G(V,E)$ as input, where $d[v]$ and $f[v]$ are the discovery time and finishing time, respectively, of the vertex $v \in V$.

Suppose that the input directed graph $G(V,E)$ is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

For an edge $(u,v)\in E$, which of the following options will NEVER be correct?

code.text:
DFS(G):
  unmark all v in V
  t <- 0
  for each v in V
    if v is unmarked
      t <- Explore(G, v, t)
    end if
  end for

Explore(G, v, t):
  mark v
  t <- t + 1
  d[v] <- t
  for each (v, w) in E
    if w is unmarked
      t <- Explore(G, w, t)
    end if
  end for
  t <- t + 1
  f[v] <- t
  return t

solutionDiagram.alt: Four pairs of interval bars for u and v showing nested, disjoint and partially overlapping orders, with B and D marked as never possible in a DAG.

steps.title: Definitions and the nesting rule
steps.body: In DFS, $d[v]$ is the time the vertex is first reached and $f[v]$ the time its exploration ends; the clock ticks once at each. The interval $[d[v],f[v]]$ is when $v$ is on the recursion stack. Two such intervals are either nested (one vertex is a descendant of the other) or disjoint; they never partly overlap, because a vertex that starts inside another must finish before it. Edge $(u,v)$ is classified by how the intervals sit: $v$ inside $u$ is a tree or forward edge, $v$ before $u$ and disjoint is a cross edge, and $u$ inside $v$ is a back edge. A DAG has no cycle, so a back edge cannot exist.

steps.title: Classify the four options
steps.body: (A) $d[u]<d[v]<f[v]<f[u]$: $v$ nested inside $u$. A tree or forward edge. Possible. (B) $d[v]<d[u]<f[u]<f[v]$: $u$ nested inside $v$. That is a back edge; $v$ is an ancestor of $u$ and $u\to v$ closes a cycle. Never in a DAG. (C) $d[v]<f[v]<d[u]<f[u]$: disjoint, $v$ finished before $u$ began. A cross edge. Possible. (D) $d[u]<d[v]<f[u]<f[v]$: the intervals partly overlap. DFS never produces this, for any graph.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Options B and D can never be correct, so the answer is B and D.

shortcut.body: Draw each option as two bars. Nested or disjoint is allowed; partly overlapping is impossible (D). Nested with $v$ outside is a back edge, impossible in a DAG (B).

traps.text: Marking A as impossible: it looks like the 'normal' tree-edge pattern, so it is always possible, not never.
Marking C as impossible because cross edges feel unusual. In a DAG they are allowed: the edge leads to a vertex already finished.
Picking only B. D is easy to miss because partial overlap looks harmless, but the parenthesis structure of DFS forbids it in every graph.

recognize.clues: The question gives discovery and finishing times and asks which orderings of the four times are impossible for an edge in a DAG. That is classifying edges by interval nesting.
recognize.contrast: A back edge has the interval of its target wrapped around the interval of its source, while a cross edge has the target finished before the source starts. Only the first needs a cycle.

check.body: Test option D by hand with $d[u]=1$, $d[v]=2$, $f[u]=3$, $f[v]=4$. Vertex $v$ is discovered while $u$ is still being explored, so the call for $u$ cannot return until the call for $v$ has returned. That forces $f[v]<f[u]$, contradicting the pattern, whatever the graph.

variation.stem: DFS runs on the directed graph with edges $1\to2$, $1\to3$, $2\to4$, $3\to2$, $3\to4$, $4\to1$, starting at vertex 1 and always taking neighbours in increasing order. Which of the following statements is/are true?
variation.explanation: DFS goes $1\to2\to4$, finds $4\to1$ pointing to an ancestor on the stack (back edge), and backs up. It then reaches 3 from 1, so $(1,3)$ is a tree edge. From 3 the vertices 2 and 4 are already finished and not descendants of 3, so $(3,2)$ and $(3,4)$ are cross edges. A and B are true.

questions.stem:
An undirected, unweighted, simple graph $G(V,E)$ is said to be 2-colorable if there exists a function $c: V \to \{0,1\}$ such that for every $(u,v)\in E$, $c(u)\neq c(v)$.

Which of the following statements about 2-colorable graphs is/are true?
options: If $G$ is 2-colorable, then $G$ may contain cycles of odd length
If $G$ is 2-colorable, then $G$ may contain cycles of even length
An optimal algorithm for testing whether $G$ is 2-colorable runs in time $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$, if $G$ is represented as an adjacency list
An optimal algorithm for testing whether $G$ is 2-colorable runs in time $\Theta(|E|\log|V|)$, if $G$ is represented as an adjacency list

steps.title: What 2-colorable means
steps.body: Give every vertex one of two colours so that the two ends of each edge differ. Two facts decide everything. Walking around a cycle, the colours must alternate, so a cycle with an odd number of vertices would need the first and last vertex, which are neighbours, to share a colour: impossible. An even cycle alternates cleanly. So a graph is 2-colorable exactly when it has no odd cycle. A graph with such a colouring is called bipartite.

steps.title: Statements A and B
steps.body: (A) says a 2-colorable graph may contain an odd cycle. A triangle needs three colours, so it cannot be 2-coloured, and no graph holding an odd cycle can be. A is false. (B) says it may contain an even cycle. The 4-cycle with colours $0,1,0,1$ works. B is true.

steps.title: Statements C and D
steps.body: To test, start BFS from an uncoloured vertex, colour it $0$, and give each newly found neighbour the opposite colour. If an edge ever joins two vertices of the same colour, the graph is not 2-colorable; otherwise it is. Every vertex is dequeued once and every adjacency-list entry scanned once, so the cost is $\Theta(|V|+|E|)$. Reading the input is already $\Omega(|V|+|E|)$, so this is optimal and C is true. D claims $\Theta(|E|\log|V|)$, which is larger and so not the optimal bound. The true statements are B and C.

shortcut.body: Odd cycle means no 2-colouring, so A is false and B true. BFS or DFS colouring is linear, so C. Anything with a log is not optimal here.

traps.text: Statement A: odd cycles are exactly what 2-colouring forbids. A single triangle is the standard witness.
Statement D: a log factor would come from sorting or a heap, which the colouring test never needs. BFS alone is linear.

recognize.clues: The question asks for an optimal test of 2-colourability on an adjacency list. A BFS layer by layer, giving neighbours the opposite colour, does this in one pass over the lists.
recognize.contrast: A DFS would colour just as well and cost the same, so the choice of traversal is not the point. Do not confuse 2-colouring, which is easy, with colouring using 3 or more colours, which is hard.

check.body: Use a second route: count the work. On the 4-cycle the adjacency lists hold $2|E|=8$ entries and there are 4 dequeues, so the traversal does $|V|+2|E|=12$ steps, proportional to $|V|+|E|$. For the cycle test, colour a 5-cycle $a,b,c,d,e$ as 0, 1, 0, 1, 0 and the closing edge $e$ to $a$ joins two 0s, a clash; the 4-cycle closes with 1 against 0 and passes. Odd length forces the clash.

options: The 6-cycle with an extra edge joining vertices 1 and 3

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph $G$ is/are TRUE?
options: A DFS tree of $G$ is a Shortest Path tree of $G$.
Every non-tree edge of $G$ with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.
If $(u,v)$ is a non-tree edge of $G$ with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from the source vertex $s$ to $u$ and $v$ in the BFS tree are within $\pm 1$ of each other.
Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of $G$.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A BFS tree grows level by level from the source $s$; the level of a vertex is its edge-count distance from $s$. A DFS tree plunges as deep as possible before backing up. A non-tree edge is a graph edge that the traversal did not use to discover a vertex. A shortest-path tree is a spanning tree in which the tree path from $s$ to each vertex has the fewest possible edges. Two rules decide the question. In an undirected graph a DFS never produces a cross edge: every non-tree edge joins a vertex to one of its ancestors. In BFS every edge joins vertices whose levels differ by at most 1.

steps.title: Statements A and B
steps.body: (A) A DFS tree is a shortest-path tree. False: in a triangle $s,a,b$ DFS may go $s\to a\to b$, giving $b$ depth 2 although $b$ is adjacent to $s$. (B) Every non-tree edge of a DFS tree is a forward or back edge. Suppose a non-tree edge joined two vertices in different branches. The earlier-finished one would have found the other while it was still unvisited and made it a descendant. So every non-tree edge links an ancestor and a descendant; seen from the descendant it is a back edge, seen from the ancestor a forward edge. True.

steps.title: Statements C and D
steps.body: (C) Let $(u,v)$ be a non-tree edge in a BFS tree with $d(u)\le d(v)$ from $s$. When $u$ is processed, $v$ is either already discovered or gets discovered through $u$, so $d(v)\le d(u)+1$. Hence $|d(u)-d(v)|\le 1$. True. (D) Running BFS or DFS from an unvisited vertex reaches exactly its connected component; repeating for each unvisited vertex lists all components. True. The true statements are B, C and D.

shortcut.body: Kill A with a triangle (DFS gives depth 2 to a neighbour of the source). B, C and D are standard facts: no cross edges in undirected DFS, BFS levels differ by at most 1, both traversals find components.

traps.text: Choosing A confuses BFS with DFS. Only BFS yields shortest paths in an unweighted graph; DFS depth can be far larger than the true distance.

questions.stem:
Let $G$ be an edge-weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights. Suppose a positive constant $\alpha$ is added to the weight of every edge.

Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE about the minimum spanning trees (MSTs) and shortest paths (SPs) in $G$ before and after the edge weight update?
options: Every MST remains an MST, and every SP remains an SP.
MSTs need not remain MSTs, and every SP remains an SP.
Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.
MSTs need not remain MSTs, and SPs need not remain SPs.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two copies of a triangle s, a, t: before adding 2 the route through a costs 2 against 3, after adding 2 the direct edge costs 5 against 6.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a set of $|V|-1$ edges that connects all vertices with the least total weight. A shortest path (SP) from $s$ to $t$ is a path of least total weight. Adding $\alpha$ to every edge changes the total of a set of edges by $\alpha$ times the number of edges in the set. The question is whether the best set stays the best. It does when every competitor has the same number of edges, and it does not when the competitors have different numbers.

steps.title: Spanning trees
steps.body: Every spanning tree has exactly $|V|-1$ edges, so each tree's weight rises by the same amount $(|V|-1)\alpha$. The order of the trees by weight is unchanged, so every MST stays an MST.

steps.title: Shortest paths
steps.body: Paths between $s$ and $t$ can have different numbers of edges, so a path with $k$ edges rises by $k\alpha$. Take a direct edge $s\to t$ of weight 3 and a route $s\to a\to t$ of weights 1 and 1, total 2. The two-edge route is the SP. With $\alpha=2$ the direct edge costs 5 and the route costs 6, so the SP changes. SPs need not remain SPs. The answer is (C).

shortcut.body: Spanning trees all have $|V|-1$ edges, so MSTs survive a uniform shift. Paths differ in edge count, so SPs can flip. One three-vertex example proves it.

traps.text: Choosing A trusts that a uniform shift is harmless for paths too. It is harmless only when the compared objects have equal edge counts.
Choosing B reverses the facts: SPs are the ones that break, MSTs are the ones that survive.
Choosing D thinks MSTs break under a shift. Edge counts match across spanning trees, so they cannot.

recognize.clues: The same positive constant is added to every weight and the question asks what survives for MSTs and for shortest paths. All spanning trees have the same edge count, whereas paths between two vertices do not.
recognize.contrast: A shortest path depends on the sum over a variable number of edges, so a uniform shift can reorder routes. An MST compares fixed-size edge sets, so a uniform shift cannot.

check.body: Take a triangle with weights 1, 2 and 3. The MST drops the edge of weight 3. Add 10 to every edge to get 11, 12 and 13, and the MST still drops the heaviest edge, 13. The tree order is the same because both trees have 2 edges.

questions.stem:
Consider the following algorithm someAlgo that takes an undirected graph $G$ as input.

someAlgo($G$)
1. Let $v$ be any vertex in $G$. Run BFS on $G$ starting at $v$. Let $u$ be a vertex in $G$ at maximum distance from $v$ as given by the BFS.
2. Run BFS on $G$ again with $u$ as the starting vertex. Let $z$ be the vertex at maximum distance from $u$ as given by the BFS.
3. Output the distance between $u$ and $z$ in $G$.

The output of someAlgo($T$) for the tree shown in the given figure is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.figure: A tree with 14 vertices, which this solution numbers 1 to 14 (the paper does not number them). Edges: 1-2, 2-3, 2-5, 4-5, 5-6, 6-7, 5-8, 8-9, 8-10, 8-11, 11-12, 11-13, 13-14. Vertices 5 and 8 have degree 4.

diagram.alt: Tree with 14 numbered vertices and 13 edges, two hubs at vertices 5 and 8.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same tree with the longest path from vertex 14 to vertex 7 drawn thick and the distances from vertex 14, 0 to 6, along it.

steps.title: What the algorithm computes
steps.body: BFS from a start vertex labels every vertex with its distance, the number of edges on the path to it. A tree has exactly one path between any two vertices, so distance is the length of that path. The diameter of a tree is the longest distance between any two vertices. someAlgo is the classic two-sweep method: any start $v$, then the farthest vertex $u$ from it, then the farthest vertex $z$ from $u$, and output $d(u,z)$. On a tree this equals the diameter, because the farthest vertex from any start is always an end of some longest path.

steps.title: Read the tree
steps.body: Label the vertices as in the drawing. The edges are 1-2, 2-3, 2-5, 4-5, 5-6, 6-7, 5-8, 8-9, 8-10, 8-11, 11-12, 11-13, 13-14. Vertex 5 and vertex 8 are the two hubs; the long chain is 7-6-5-8-11-13-14, and the branch 1-2-5 gives a second chain of the same length.

steps.title: Run the two sweeps
steps.body: Start at $v=5$: distances are 1 to {2,4,6,8}, 2 to {1,3,7,9,10,11}, 3 to {12,13}, 4 to 14. The farthest vertex is $u=14$. BFS from 14 gives 13 at 1, 11 at 2, {8,12} at 3, {5,9,10} at 4, {2,4,6} at 5 and {1,3,7} at 6. The farthest is at distance 6, for example $z=7$. The output is 6, which is also the diameter, and the same value comes out for every start vertex.

shortcut.body: On a tree the answer is the diameter. Find the two ends of the longest chain by eye: 7 to 14 passes through 6, 5, 8, 11, 13, so 6 edges.

traps.text: Answering 7 by counting vertices on the longest path (7 vertices) instead of edges. Distance counts edges.

Answering 5 or 4 by stopping short of the far end. Stopping at 6 instead of 7 gives the 5-edge chain 6-5-8-11-13-14, and measuring only from the hub 5 gives 4. The chain 1-2-5-8-11-13-14 also has 6 edges, so the diameter is 6 either way.

recognize.clues: The algorithm runs BFS twice, the second time from the farthest vertex of the first, on a tree. Distances in a tree are unique path lengths, so the output is the longest distance in the tree.
recognize.contrast: The first sweep alone only gives the farthest vertex from the chosen start, which may be shorter than the diameter. On a graph with cycles the two-sweep method is not exact, so do not carry it beyond trees.

check.body: Run a third BFS from vertex 7 in the solution numbering. Its farthest vertex is 14, at distance 6 along 7-6-5-8-11-13-14, and no vertex is farther. This agrees with the answer from the two sweeps, which is a check from a different start.

questions.stem: Let $G$ be any undirected graph with positive edge weights, and $T$ be a minimum spanning tree of $G$. For any two vertices, $u$ and $v$, let $d_1(u,v)$ and $d_2(u,v)$ be the shortest distances between $u$ and $v$ in $G$ and $T$, respectively. Which ONE of the options is CORRECT for all possible $G$, $T$, $u$ and $v$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Triangle u, v, w with weights 1, 1.5 and 2 where the thick MST path from u to v has weight 2.5 and the dashed direct edge weighs 2.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: The shortest distance between $u$ and $v$ in a graph is the least total weight over all paths joining them in that graph. A minimum spanning tree $T$ is a subgraph of $G$: it uses only edges of $G$, though not all of them. The rule: a minimum over a bigger set of paths is never larger than a minimum over a smaller set.

steps.title: Compare the two path sets
steps.body: Every path in $T$ is also a path in $G$, so $G$ has all the candidates $T$ has, plus possibly more. Hence the best path in $G$ is no longer than the best in $T$.

steps.title: Equality is not guaranteed
steps.body: The MST minimises total weight, not individual distances. Take $u,v,w$ with $uw=1$, $wv=1.5$, $uv=2$. The MST drops the heaviest edge $uv$, so $d_2(u,v)=2.5$ while $d_1(u,v)=2$. So $=$ and $\ge$ fail, and $\ne$ fails whenever $T$ keeps the direct edge. Only (B) always holds.

shortcut.body: $T\subseteq G$ so $G$ offers more paths: $d_1\le d_2$. Check equality with a triangle if tempted.

traps.text: Choosing equality because the MST 'connects everything cheaply'. It minimises total weight, not each pair's distance; the triangle $1,1.5,2$ gives $2\ne 2.5$.
Choosing $d_1\ge d_2$ reverses the subgraph logic. $T$ has fewer paths, so its distance can only be larger or equal.
Choosing $d_1\ne d_2$ fails when $u,v$ are joined by an edge that lies in $T$; then both distances are equal.

recognize.clues: The question compares distances in a graph with distances in its minimum spanning tree and asks what holds for every graph. That is a question about what a spanning tree preserves, which is total weight and not pairwise distance.
recognize.contrast: Shortest-path trees preserve distances from one root, while an MST only minimises total weight. Do not carry the shortest-path property over to the MST.

check.body: If $G$ is itself a tree then $T=G$ and the two distances are equal for every pair, so a strict relation between them cannot hold for all graphs. Take the triangle with sides $1,1.5,2$: the edge of weight 2 is not in the MST, so $d_1=2$ while the tree path gives $d_2=1+1.5=2.5$. An extra edge no lighter than the tree edges on its cycle but lighter than the tree path gives $d_1<d_2$, which fixes the direction of the inequality.

questions.stem: Let $G(V,E)$ be an undirected and unweighted graph with 100 vertices. Let $d(u,v)$ denote the number of edges in a shortest path between vertices $u$ and $v$ in $V$. Let the maximum value of $d(u,v)$, $u,v\in V$ such that $u\neq v$, be 30. Let $T$ be any breadth-first-search tree of $G$. Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such graph $G$?
options: The height of $T$ is at least 15.
The height of $T$ is at least 30.

solutionDiagram.alt: A path of 31 vertices with the root marked at the middle, showing the endpoints 30 apart and each end 15 away from the root.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A BFS tree rooted at $r$ places each vertex at depth equal to its distance from $r$, so the height of $T$ is the eccentricity of $r$, the largest $d(r,x)$ over all $x$. The largest distance in the whole graph, 30 here, is called the diameter. The rule that links them is the triangle inequality: $d(u,v)\le d(u,r)+d(r,v)$.

steps.title: Lower bound on the height
steps.body: Pick $u,v$ with $d(u,v)=30$. Then $30\le d(r,u)+d(r,v)$, so at least one of the two distances is at least 15. Therefore the height of $T$, which is at least that distance, is at least 15 for any root.

steps.title: Why it can be anything from 15 to 30
steps.body: Take a path of 31 vertices and hang the other 69 vertices as leaves on its middle vertex, so the diameter is still 30. Rooted at the middle, the BFS height is 15; rooted at an end, it is 30. So the height is not forced to equal 15 or 30, and 'at least 30' fails. The only statement true for every such graph is 'at least 15', option (C).

shortcut.body: Height $\ge$ half the diameter, by the triangle inequality. Test 'exactly' and 'at least 30' on a path with the root in the middle.

traps.text: Choosing 'exactly 15' because the best root gives 15. The tree may be rooted anywhere, and an end root gives 30.
Choosing 'exactly 30' because the diameter is 30. A central root gives a shorter tree.
Choosing 'at least 30' mixes up the height of one BFS tree with the diameter. Only the farthest pair is 30 apart.

recognize.clues: The question speaks of a BFS tree, its height and the maximum shortest distance in the graph, and asks for what holds for every such graph. BFS depth equals shortest distance, so height equals eccentricity of the root.
recognize.contrast: A DFS tree has no such link to distances and can be far taller than the diameter. Only BFS ties tree depth to graph distance.

check.body: Use a path of 31 vertices, diameter 30. A root at the centre gives height 15, a root one step off centre gives 16, and an end gives 30. No root gives less than 15, which agrees with the triangle bound and shows 15 is reachable but not forced.

steps.title: Definitions and the cut rule
steps.body: A minimum spanning tree (MST) connects all vertices with the least total weight and no cycle. A cut splits the vertices into two groups. The cut rule: the lightest edge crossing a cut is in the MST, and if it is the only lightest edge across that cut, it is in every MST. If two crossing edges tie for lightest, either one can be chosen, so neither is forced.

steps.title: Build the MST without B-C
steps.body: Edges: A-B 7, A-D 6, D-C 8, B-C $x$, B-D 1, A-C 3. The two lightest, B-D (1) and A-C (3), cannot be avoided: B-D is the lightest edge at B and D, A-C (3) is the lightest edge at A, whose other edges are A-B 7 and A-D 6, so it is the lightest edge across the cut of A alone against the rest, and they form no cycle. They leave two groups {B,D} and {A,C}.

steps.title: Cheapest edge between the two groups
steps.body: The edges across are A-B 7, A-D 6, D-C 8 and B-C $x$. B-C is in every MST exactly when it is strictly cheaper than all the others, that is $x<6$. At $x=6$ it ties with A-D and an MST can use A-D instead. The largest integer with $x<6$ is 5.

shortcut.body: Keep the forced edges 1 and 3, then B-C must beat the cheapest other crossing edge 6. Strictly less, so 5 for integers.

traps.text: Answering 6: at $x=6$ B-C ties with A-D, and an MST using A-D exists, so B-C is not in every MST.
Answering 7 or 8 by comparing only with A-B or D-C and forgetting A-D, the cheapest crossing edge.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the largest value of an edge weight that keeps one specific edge in every minimum spanning tree. The words every MST point to the cut property with strict inequality, not to one run of Kruskal.
recognize.contrast: Kruskal and Prim each build one MST, so they can hide ties. A statement about every MST needs the strict cut condition, because a tie lets another edge take over.

check.body: Set the weight to 5 and run Kruskal. The edges 1 and 3 are taken, then the weight-5 edge joins the two groups, and the weight-6 edge is rejected as a cycle, so the tree weighs 9. At weight 6 the A-D edge ties with it, and Kruskal may take A-D first, giving an equally light tree without B-C, so it is no longer forced.

steps.title: Definitions and the counting idea
steps.body: A spanning tree joins all $n$ vertices with $n-1$ edges and no cycle. A minimum-weight spanning tree (MST) is one with the least total weight. Kruskal's method sorts edges by weight and takes each edge that does not close a cycle. Edges of equal weight can be taken in any order, so ties are where several different MSTs come from. To count MSTs, process each weight class and count the ways to pick edges that join the current pieces without a cycle.

steps.title: Weight 1 edges
steps.body: The graph has 7 vertices, so each MST has 6 edges. The weight-1 edges are a-b, a-f, c-d and d-e. They form no cycle, so all four are taken. The pieces are {a,b,f}, {c,d,e} and {g}.

steps.title: Weight 2 edges
steps.body: The weight-2 edges are a-g, b-g, f-g (joining g to the left piece) and c-g, d-g, e-g (joining g to the right piece). Two more edges are needed to join three pieces. Exactly one must link g to the left piece and one to the right piece; taking two on the same side would close a cycle. That gives 3 choices on each side.

steps.title: Weight 3 edges and the total
steps.body: The weight-3 edges b-c and e-f would join pieces that are already connected, so they are never used. Every MST has weight $4\cdot 1+2\cdot 2=8$. The count of MSTs is 9.

shortcut.body: Take the four weight-1 edges, then g needs one weight-2 edge into each three-vertex side: $3\times3=9$. Ignore the weight-3 edges.

traps.text: Answering 6 by counting 3 + 3 (adding the choices instead of multiplying). The two choices are independent, so they multiply.
Answering 15 by choosing any 2 of the 6 weight-2 edges, $\binom{6}{2}=15$. Six of those pairs lie on one side and close a cycle through g, leaving $15-6=9$.

questions.stem: Let $G$ be a directed graph and $T$ a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in $G$ that is rooted at a vertex $v$. Suppose $T$ is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in $G$, rooted at $v$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph $G$ and tree $T$ ?
options: There are no back-edges in $G$ with respect to the tree $T$
There are no cross-edges in $G$ with respect to the tree $T$
There are no forward-edges in $G$ with respect to the tree $T$
The only edges in $G$ are the edges in $T$

solutionDiagram.alt: A root v with children a and b and a child c of a, with a dashed back edge from a to v, a dashed cross edge from b to a, and a crossed-out forward edge from v to c.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Given a spanning tree $T$ rooted at $v$, every non-tree edge $(x,y)$ of the directed graph falls into one of three kinds. A back edge goes from a vertex to one of its ancestors in $T$. A forward edge goes from a vertex to a descendant that is not its child. A cross edge joins two vertices where neither is an ancestor of the other. $T$ is a BFS tree when each vertex's depth in $T$ equals its shortest-path distance from $v$. $T$ is a DFS tree when some DFS run produces it.

steps.title: Forward edges are impossible
steps.body: Suppose $(x,y)$ is a forward edge. Then $y$ is a descendant of $x$ at depth at least $\text{depth}(x)+2$. But the edge itself gives a path $v\to x\to y$ of length $\text{depth}(x)+1$, so $y$'s BFS distance is smaller than its tree depth. That contradicts $T$ being a BFS tree. So (C) holds for every such graph.

steps.title: Back and cross edges are possible
steps.body: Back edge: take $v\to a$ as the only tree edge and add $a\to v$. The tree is both a DFS and a BFS tree and has a back edge, so (A) is not forced. Cross edge: tree edges $v\to a$ and $v\to b$, plus the edge $b\to a$. DFS may visit $a$ first, then $b$, and $b\to a$ goes to a finished non-ancestor. Depths are 1 and 1, matching BFS. So (B) fails. (D) is false for the same examples, which have extra edges. Only (C) is true.

shortcut.body: Forward edge means a descendant at depth two or more reached by a direct edge, which BFS would have placed higher. Back and cross edges are shown with a two- and a three-vertex example.

traps.text: Statement A: the edge $a\to v$ in a two-vertex example is a back edge and the tree is still both DFS and BFS.
Statement B: with children $a,b$ of $v$ and an edge $b\to a$, DFS visiting $a$ first makes it a cross edge, and depths match BFS.
Statement D: the extra edges in the examples above show $G$ need not be just $T$.

recognize.clues: The question asks which non-tree edge kinds are absent when one tree is both a DFS tree and a BFS tree, so it is about classifying edges by their position relative to the tree.
recognize.contrast: In a DFS tree on an undirected graph there are no cross edges, but here the graph is directed, so cross edges are allowed and the BFS depth rule must decide each case.

check.body: For the statement about edges skipping down the tree, take the path $v\to a\to b$ and add $v\to b$. The vertex $b$ then has distance 1 but tree depth 2, so $T$ is no longer a BFS tree. That confirms the depth rule rules the edge out.

recognize.clues: The question gives the number of edges of the DFS forest and the number of vertices, and asks for the number of components. The forest has one tree per component, which turns the count into a counting relation.
recognize.contrast: The edge count of the graph itself is not the forest edge count. Only the tree edges are counted here, and extra edges of the graph play no role.

check.body: Test the extremes. With one component the forest has $100-1=99$ edges and with 100 isolated vertices it has 0. Each extra component removes one edge, so 40 edges is $99-40=59$ extra components above the first, which makes 60.

questions.stem:
Let $U = \{1, 2, 3\}$. Let $2^U$ denote the powerset of $U$. Consider an undirected graph $G$ whose vertex set is $2^U$. For any $A, B \in 2^U$, $(A, B)$ is an edge in $G$ if and only if (i) $A 
eq B$, and (ii) either $A \subsetneq B$ or $B \subsetneq A$. For any vertex $A$ in $G$, the set of all possible orderings in which the vertices of $G$ can be visited in a Breadth First Search (BFS) starting from $A$ is denoted by $\mathcal{B}(A)$.

If $\emptyset$ denotes the empty set, then the cardinality of $\mathcal{B}(\emptyset)$ is ____.

solutionDiagram.alt: The empty set at the centre joined to the seven other subsets of {1,2,3}: {1}, {2}, {3}, {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3} and {1,2,3}, all at BFS layer 1.

steps.title: What a BFS ordering is
steps.body: Breadth First Search (BFS) starts at a vertex $s$ and uses a queue, first in and first out. It visits $s$, then every neighbour of $s$ (layer 1), then every vertex first reached from those neighbours (layer 2), and so on. When a vertex has several undiscovered neighbours, the algorithm may put them into the queue in any order, and each choice gives a different visiting order. So $|\mathcal{B}(s)|$ counts the different sequences BFS can produce. The rule that decides this question: once a vertex is taken from the queue, all of its undiscovered neighbours enter the queue together, in any order you like.

steps.title: Read the graph
steps.body: $U=\{1,2,3\}$ has $2^3=8$ subsets, so $G$ has 8 vertices. Two different subsets are joined exactly when one is a proper subset of the other. The empty set is a proper subset of every non-empty set, so $\emptyset$ is joined to all 7 other vertices: $\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{1,2,3\}$. Edges also join some of these seven to each other, but that will not matter.

steps.title: Count the orderings from the empty set
steps.body: BFS starts at $\emptyset$ and takes it off the queue first. All 7 other vertices are undiscovered neighbours of $\emptyset$, so all 7 enter the queue at once, in any order. After that, every vertex is already discovered, so nothing more is added and the visiting order is simply the queue order. Each of the $7!$ arrangements is possible, and two different arrangements are two different visiting orders. So $|\mathcal{B}(\emptyset)|=7!=5040$.

shortcut.body: If the start vertex is adjacent to every other vertex, the whole graph is layer 1 and the answer is $(n-1)!$ with $n=8$ vertices, so $7!=5040$. It takes 20 seconds once you see that $\emptyset$ is a subset of everything.

traps.text: Answering $8! = 40320$ by letting all 8 vertices be ordered freely. The start vertex is fixed as the first vertex visited, so only the other 7 are arranged.

Drawing only the edges that add one element at a time (the Hasse diagram of the powerset). The question's edge rule is any proper subset relation, so $\emptyset$ is joined directly to $\{1,2,3\}$ as well, and layer 1 holds all 7 vertices.
Answering 7, the number of neighbours, or 8, the number of vertices. The question counts orderings, not vertices.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the number of different BFS visiting orders from a given start vertex. The start vertex is a subset of every other vertex, so it is adjacent to the whole graph.
recognize.contrast: DFS orders depend on how deep each choice goes, while BFS orders depend only on how neighbours are enqueued layer by layer. A star-like start has a single layer, so only one factorial appears.

check.body: Shrink the problem to $U=\{1,2\}$, with 4 vertices. From the empty set the other three enter the queue together and can be ordered in $3!=6$ ways. Enumerating every BFS run by script gives 6, and the same enumeration for $U=\{1,2,3\}$ gives 5040.

questions.stem: Consider a simple undirected weighted graph $G$, all of whose edge weights are distinct. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees of $G$ is/are TRUE?
options: The edge with the second smallest weight is always part of any minimum spanning tree of $G$.
One or both of the edges with the third smallest and the fourth smallest weights are part of any minimum spanning tree of $G$.

Suppose $S \subseteq V$ be such that $S \neq \phi$ and $S \neq V$. Consider the edge with the minimum weight such that one of its vertices is in $S$ and the other in $V \setminus S$. Such an edge will always be part of any minimum spanning tree of $G$.
$G$ can have multiple minimum spanning trees.

steps.title: Terms and the two rules
steps.body: A spanning tree of a connected graph uses every vertex, is connected and has no cycle, so it has $|V|-1$ edges. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree of least total weight. A simple graph has no loops and no two edges between the same pair of vertices, so every cycle has at least 3 edges. A cut splits the vertices into $S$ and $V\setminus S$; an edge crosses it if its ends lie on different sides. Rule 1, the cut property: with distinct weights, the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to every MST. Rule 2, the cycle property: the heaviest edge of any cycle belongs to no MST.

steps.title: Statement (C) is Rule 1
steps.body: (C) names a cut $(S, V\setminus S)$ and the lightest edge crossing it. Weights are distinct, so that edge is unique and, by the cut property, it lies in every MST. (C) is true.

steps.title: Statement (A): the second smallest edge
steps.body: Call the edges in increasing weight $e_1<e_2<e_3<e_4<\dots$. An edge stays out of an MST only if it is the heaviest edge of some cycle. For $e_2$ that cycle would need at least two edges lighter than $e_2$, because a cycle has at least 3 edges, but only $e_1$ is lighter. So $e_2$ is in every MST, and (A) is true. The same argument puts $e_1$ in every MST.

steps.title: Statement (B): the third or fourth smallest
steps.body: Run Kruskal's method: take edges in increasing order and skip an edge that closes a cycle. It accepts $e_1$ and $e_2$ by (A). If it accepts $e_3$, (B) already holds. It skips $e_3$ only if $e_3$ closes a cycle with already accepted edges, that is a triangle $e_1,e_2,e_3$. Then $e_4$ would close a cycle only with accepted edges $\{e_1,e_2\}$, which would be a triangle $e_1,e_2,e_4$. But $e_1,e_2$ form a path of two edges and a simple graph has just one edge joining its two ends, namely $e_3$. So $e_4\ne e_3$ cannot join those ends, and $e_4$ is accepted. At least one of $e_3,e_4$ is always in the MST, so (B) is true.

steps.title: Statement (D): uniqueness
steps.body: Take any MST $T$ and delete one tree edge $e$. The tree falls into two parts, a cut. $e$ must be the lightest edge crossing that cut, otherwise swapping in the lighter one would lower the weight. With distinct weights that lightest edge is unique, so by Rule 1 every MST contains $e$. Applying this to every edge of $T$ shows every MST contains all of $T$, so all MSTs equal $T$. $G$ has exactly one MST and (D) is false. The answer is (A), (B), (C).

shortcut.body: (C) is the cut property word for word. (A) and (B) are Kruskal's first four steps: a cycle needs 3 edges, so $e_2$ cannot be the heaviest edge of any cycle, and $e_3,e_4$ cannot both be rejected. (D) is false because distinct weights force a unique MST. The reasoning for (A) and (B) needs the graph to be simple, with no parallel edges.

traps.text: Selecting (D) because many graphs have several MSTs. That needs equal weights, which this graph does not have. Distinct weights give exactly one MST.
Leaving out (A) because 'always part of any MST' sounds too strong. It holds here because no cycle in a simple graph can have $e_2$ as its heaviest edge.
Leaving out (B) because $e_3$ can be rejected by Kruskal. 'One or both' allows that case, and $e_4$ is then accepted.
Leaving out (C) because the lightest crossing edge looks like it could depend on the chosen set $S$. The cut property holds for every non-trivial $S$ when weights are distinct.

recognize.clues: Every statement is a claim about which edges lie in the minimum spanning trees of a graph with distinct weights. The cut rule and the cycle rule decide each claim.
recognize.contrast: When weights may repeat, a tie can swap one edge for another and several MSTs exist. Distinctness is what makes the cut edge forced and the tree unique.

check.body: Take a triangle with weights 1, 2, 3 and a pendant edge of weight 4. Kruskal keeps 1, 2 and 4 and rejects 3. The second smallest is kept and the fourth is kept when the third is rejected. There is exactly one MST here, which matches the uniqueness argument.

questions.stem:
Let $G$ be a connected undirected weighted graph. Consider the following two statements.

$S_1$: There exists a minimum weight edge in $G$ which is present in every minimum spanning tree of $G$.
$S_2$: If every edge in $G$ has distinct weight, then $G$ has a unique minimum spanning tree.

Which one of the following options is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Three copies of a triangle x, y, z with all weights 1. Each copy keeps two edges and omits a different third edge, so the three minimum spanning trees share no edge.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A spanning tree connects all vertices with no cycle; a minimum spanning tree (MST) has the least total weight. A minimum weight edge is an edge whose weight equals the smallest weight in the graph. The rule that settles both statements is the cut property: for any split of the vertices into two sides, a lightest edge crossing the split can be taken into some MST, and if that lightest crossing edge is unique, every MST contains it. Equal weights are where choices, and so several MSTs, appear.

steps.title: Test $S_2$
steps.body: With all weights distinct, every cut has a unique lightest crossing edge. Take an MST $T$ and delete one of its edges: the two pieces form a cut, and the deleted edge must be the lightest edge across it, since otherwise a swap would lower the weight. It is then the unique lightest edge, so every MST contains it. This holds for every edge of $T$, so every MST contains $T$ and equals $T$. $S_2$ is true.

steps.title: Test $S_1$ with a counterexample
steps.body: Take a triangle on $x,y,z$ with all three weights equal to 1. A spanning tree of 3 vertices has 2 edges, so each pair of edges is an MST of weight 2: there are 3 MSTs, and each one omits a different edge. Every edge has the minimum weight 1, yet each edge is missing from some MST, so no minimum weight edge lies in every MST. $S_1$ is false. $S_1$ would be true if the lightest edge were unique, but the statement does not say that. $S_1$ false and $S_2$ true is option (C).

shortcut.body: Try the smallest graph with ties, a triangle of equal weights: it kills $S_1$ in 20 seconds. $S_2$ is the textbook fact that distinct weights give a unique MST. Only option (C) has $S_1$ false and $S_2$ true.

traps.text: Believing $S_1$ because 'the lightest edge is always in the MST'. That is true when the lightest edge is unique; with ties some lightest edge can be left out of a particular MST, and no single one is in all of them.
Accepting $S_1$ and rejecting $S_2$ is the reverse of the truth. Distinct weights make every cut's lightest edge unique, which forces one MST.
Rejecting $S_2$ because several MSTs exist in many graphs. They exist only when equal weights create ties.

recognize.clues: Two universal claims about all minimum spanning trees of a connected weighted graph, one about a minimum weight edge and one about distinct weights, which is the language of uniqueness and ties.
recognize.contrast: This is not a question about running Kruskal or Prim to get a weight; those algorithms find one tree, while here you must reason about all minimum spanning trees at once.

check.body: Test the second statement by substitution. Take a triangle with weights 1, 2 and 3. Its three spanning trees weigh 3, 4 and 5, so exactly one tree is minimum. With a tie, as in the triangle of equal weights, all three trees weigh the same, which is why only the first statement fails.

questions.stem:
Consider the following directed graph:

Which of the following is/are correct about the graph?

diagram.alt: Directed 4 by 4 grid graph of sixteen vertices with arrows on all 24 edges and the start vertex S at the bottom left corner.

options: The graph does not have a topological order.
A depth-first traversal starting at vertex $S$ classifies three directed edges as back edges.
The graph does not have a strongly connected component.
For each pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, there is a directed path from $u$ to $v$.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same grid with three directed 4-cycles A, B and C drawn in bold and one dashed back edge in each cycle, found by a DFS from S.

steps.title: Terms and rules
steps.body: A directed cycle is a closed walk that follows arrows and returns to its start. A topological order lists all vertices so that every edge points from an earlier vertex to a later one; it exists exactly when there is no directed cycle. A strongly connected component (SCC) is a largest set of vertices in which every vertex can reach every other along arrows; a single vertex alone also counts as an SCC. In a depth-first search (DFS) an edge $u\to v$ is a back edge when $v$ is an ancestor of $u$, that is $v$ is still on the current recursion path. Every directed cycle contains a back edge, and a graph with no cycle has none.

steps.title: Find the cycles by reading the arrows
steps.body: Follow the arrows in each 2 by 2 block. Bottom left: $(3,1)\to(4,1)\to(4,2)\to(3,2)\to(3,1)$, call it cycle A. Bottom right: $(3,3)\to(4,3)\to(4,4)\to(3,4)\to(3,3)$, cycle B. Top middle: $(1,2)\to(2,2)\to(2,3)\to(1,3)\to(1,2)$, cycle C. The other arrows only run along the outside or across the middle one way. Because cycles exist, no topological order exists: (A) is true.

steps.title: SCCs and reachability: (C) and (D)
steps.body: The four vertices of cycle A can each reach every other one, so they form an SCC; so do B and C. Therefore the graph does have strongly connected components, and (C) is false. For (D), try $u=(1,1)$ and $v=S=(4,1)$. From $(1,1)$ the only way out is to $(1,2)$, then $(2,2)$, then $(2,3)$ and on to $(1,3)$, $(2,4)$, $(1,4)$. Nothing leads down to row 3, so $S$ is unreachable from $(1,1)$ and (D) is false.

steps.title: Count the back edges: (B)
steps.body: Each SCC is a plain 4-cycle, and every cycle of the graph lies inside one SCC, so there are exactly three cycles: A, B and C. The DFS from $S$ reaches all 16 vertices. Inside one 4-cycle, the first vertex DFS discovers is $v$. The other three vertices are then reached along the cycle through white vertices, so they become a chain below $v$ in the DFS tree. Only the edge that returns to $v$ is left, and it goes to an ancestor: exactly one back edge per cycle. In the run drawn, the back edges are $(2,2)\to(2,3)$, $(3,3)\to(4,3)$ and $(3,1)\to(4,1)$; another neighbour order picks a different edge of each cycle but never changes the count. Three back edges, so (B) is true. A script ran DFS from $S$ in 5000 random neighbour orders and always found 3.

shortcut.body: Spot the three one-way loops (the 2 by 2 blocks in the bottom left, bottom right and top middle). Each loop gives exactly one back edge, so (A) and (B) are true. (C) fails because those loops are SCCs, and (D) fails because from $(1,1)$ every arrow stays in rows 1 and 2, so $S$ in row 4 is never reached.

questions.stem:
In a directed acyclic graph with a source vertex $s$, the quality-score of a directed path is defined to be the product of the weights of the edges on the path. Further, for a vertex $v$ other than $s$, the quality-score of $v$ is defined to be the maximum among the quality-scores of all the paths from $s$ to $v$. The quality-score of $s$ is assumed to be 1.

The sum of the quality-scores of all the vertices in the graph shown above is ____.
questions.figure: Directed acyclic graph on nine vertices laid out in three rows. Bottom row: s, a, b. Middle row: c, d, e. Top row: f, g, t. Edges with weights: s→c 1, s→a 9, a→d 1, a→b 1, b→e 1, c→f 9, c→d 1, d→g 9, d→e 9, f→g 1, g→t 1, e→t 9.

diagram.alt: Directed acyclic graph with source s at the bottom left and edge weights 1 and 9 on twelve edges across three rows of three vertices.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same DAG with the quality-score q of every vertex: s 1, c 1, a 9, b 9, d 9, e 81, f 9, g 81, t 729, summing to 929.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) has no directed cycle, so its vertices can be listed in a topological order in which every edge goes from an earlier vertex to a later one. The quality-score $q(v)$ is the best product of edge weights over all paths from $s$ to $v$. The rule: every path to $v$ ends with one in-edge $u\to v$, so $q(v)=\max_{(u,v)}\bigl(q(u)\cdot w(u,v)\bigr)$. Weights are positive, so a larger score at $u$ always gives a larger product at $v$, and computing in topological order means every in-neighbour is already final.

steps.title: Choose a topological order
steps.body: List the vertices so every arrow points forward: $s,\ c,\ a,\ b,\ d,\ e,\ f,\ g,\ t$. Check a few arrows: $s\to c$, $c\to f$, $c\to d$, $a\to d$, $d\to g$, $f\to g$ and $e\to t$ all go from left to right.

steps.title: Compute the scores one vertex at a time
steps.body: $q(s)=1$. $c$ has the single in-edge $s\to c$ (1): $q(c)=1\cdot1=1$. $a$ has $s\to a$ (9): $q(a)=9$. $b$ has $a\to b$ (1): $q(b)=9$. $d$ has $c\to d$ (1) and $a\to d$ (1): $\max(1\cdot1,\ 9\cdot1)=9$. $e$ has $d\to e$ (9) and $b\to e$ (1): $\max(9\cdot9,\ 9\cdot1)=81$. $f$ has $c\to f$ (9): $q(f)=1\cdot9=9$. $g$ has $d\to g$ (9) and $f\to g$ (1): $\max(9\cdot9,\ 9\cdot1)=81$. $t$ has $g\to t$ (1) and $e\to t$ (9): $\max(81\cdot1,\ 81\cdot9)=729$, along $s\to a\to d\to e\to t$.

steps.title: Add the scores
steps.body: The sum over all nine vertices, including $s$ itself, is $1+1+9+9+9+81+9+81+729=929$. The answer is 929.

shortcut.body: Do the max-product pass left to right and keep the nine numbers in a column. Spot the heavy chain $s\to a\to d\to e\to t$ ($9\cdot1\cdot9\cdot9=729$) first, then fill in the others. It takes about 3 minutes; the risk is a slip in one vertex, so add the column twice.

traps.text: 928: leaving out $s$. The question says the sum over all vertices, and $q(s)=1$ is given.
281: stopping $t$ at 81 by using only the edge $g\to t$ and forgetting the heavier route through $e\to t$ with weight 9.
Adding edge weights along the path instead of multiplying them, or taking the minimum instead of the maximum at a vertex with two in-edges. The definition uses products and maxima.

recognize.clues: A directed acyclic graph with a source, a path value defined as a product of edge weights, and the best value over all paths to each vertex: a single pass in topological order.
recognize.contrast: This resembles Dijkstra, but Dijkstra needs non-negative additive weights and a priority queue; on a DAG one pass in topological order gives the optimum for products too.

check.body: Recompute in another valid order, $s,a,b,c,f,d,g,e,t$. The scores come out as $1,9,9,1,9,9,81,81,729$, which add to 929 again. The top score also matches the path $s\to a\to d\to e\to t$ with weights $9\cdot1\cdot9\cdot9=729$.

questions.stem:
Consider the following undirected graph with edge weights as shown:

The number of minimum-weight spanning trees of the graph is ____.

diagram.alt: Weighted 3 by 3 grid graph with twelve edges: seven edges of weight 0.1 and five edges of weight 0.9.

solutionDiagram.alt: The grid with the seven 0.1 edges in bold, forming a top-row tree and a six-vertex tree, and three dashed 0.9 edges that can join them, giving 3 minimum spanning trees.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A spanning tree of a graph with 9 vertices is a set of 8 edges that connects all vertices and has no cycle. A minimum-weight spanning tree (MST) has the smallest total weight. Kruskal's method builds one: look at edges from lightest to heaviest and keep an edge unless it closes a cycle. The rule for counting: every edge of the lightest weight class that closes no cycle must be used, and when two edges of equal weight could do the same job (join the same two pieces) each choice gives a different MST.

steps.title: Take all the lightest edges
steps.body: There are seven edges of weight 0.1: the top row's two edges, $(2,1)$-$(2,2)$, $(3,2)$-$(3,3)$, and the column edges $(2,1)$-$(3,1)$, $(2,2)$-$(3,2)$, $(2,3)$-$(3,3)$. Check them for cycles: the top row is a path on 3 vertices. The other six vertices are joined by five edges forming a tree: $(3,1)$-$(2,1)$-$(2,2)$-$(3,2)$-$(3,3)$-$(2,3)$, a path. No cycle, so all seven edges go into every MST, using $7\cdot0.1=0.7$ of weight. They leave two trees: Tree 1, the top row, and Tree 2, the other six vertices.

steps.title: Join the two trees with one 0.9 edge
steps.body: A spanning tree needs $9-1=8$ edges, so exactly one more edge is needed, and it must connect Tree 1 to Tree 2. The only edges left have weight 0.9. Of the five, the edges $(2,2)$-$(2,3)$ and $(3,1)$-$(3,2)$ lie inside Tree 2, so each would close a cycle. The other three, $(1,1)$-$(2,1)$, $(1,2)$-$(2,2)$ and $(1,3)$-$(2,3)$, run between the two trees. Any one of them works, and the three choices give three different trees of the same weight $0.7+0.9=1.6$. The number of MSTs is 3.

shortcut.body: Take all the lightest edges, count the pieces they leave (2), then count the heavier edges that join those two pieces (3). With two pieces and one connecting edge needed, the answer is that count, 3. Unsafe only if the 0.1 edges contain a cycle, which they do not here.

traps.text: 5: counting all five 0.9 edges as choices. Two of them join vertices already in the same tree and would form a cycle.
1: assuming an MST is unique. Three equal-weight edges connect the two pieces, so there are three trees.
12 or 7: counting edges, not trees. The question asks for the number of different minimum-weight trees.

recognize.clues: The stem asks for the number of minimum-weight spanning trees, with only two distinct weights in a grid. Counting trees means counting the tie choices.
recognize.contrast: Counting all spanning trees of a graph needs the matrix-tree theorem; here only minimum ones count, so the light edges are forced and just the tie-breaking edges are counted.

check.body: Verify by weight. A spanning tree has 8 edges, and there are only 7 light edges, so any tree weighs at least $7\cdot0.1+0.9=1.6$. The trees counted reach exactly 1.6. By inspection, each of the three top-row vertices has exactly one edge going down, all of weight 0.9, which gives the same three choices.

questions.stem:
An articulation point in a connected graph is a vertex such that removing the vertex and its incident edges disconnects the graph into two or more connected components.

Let $T$ be a DFS tree obtained by doing DFS in a connected undirected graph $G$.

Which of the following options is/are correct?
options: Root of $T$ can never be an articulation point in $G$.
Root of $T$ is an articulation point in $G$ if and only if it has 2 or more children.
A leaf of $T$ can be an articulation point in $G$.
If $u$ is an articulation point in $G$ such that $x$ is an ancestor of $u$ in $T$ and $y$ is a descendent of $u$ in $T$, then all paths from $x$ to $y$ in $G$ must pass through $u$.

solutionDiagram.alt: DFS tree with root r, child u, and u's children y and z, plus a dashed back edge from y to r. Vertex u is an articulation point but the path r to y avoids it.

steps.title: Terms and the key fact about undirected DFS
steps.body: A depth-first search (DFS) tree $T$ records, for each vertex, the vertex it was discovered from; the first vertex is the root. An articulation point is a vertex whose removal splits the graph. The key fact for undirected graphs: every edge of $G$ joins a vertex to one of its ancestors or descendants in $T$. There are no cross edges between different branches, because DFS would have walked along such an edge and put one end below the other.

steps.title: Root: (A) and (B)
steps.body: Remove the root. If it has exactly one child, the whole rest of the graph hangs below that child, and the tree $T$ minus the root is still a connected tree spanning all other vertices: the graph stays connected, so the root is not an articulation point. If the root has two or more children, there are no edges between different child subtrees (no cross edges), so after removing the root those subtrees are separated from each other. So the root is an articulation point exactly when it has at least 2 children: (B) is true. (A) is false, since a root with two children is an articulation point.

steps.title: Leaf: (C)
steps.body: Remove a leaf $\ell$ of $T$. The rest of $T$ is still a tree on all other vertices, and it uses only edges of $G$ minus $\ell$. So $G-\ell$ is connected, and a leaf of the DFS tree is never an articulation point: (C) is false.

steps.title: Statement (D) needs one counterexample
steps.body: Take vertices $r,u,y,z$ with edges $r$-$u$, $u$-$y$, $u$-$z$ and $y$-$r$, and start DFS at $r$ going to $u$, then $y$, then $z$. Tree edges: $r\to u$, $u\to y$, $u\to z$; $y$-$r$ is a back edge. Removing $u$ cuts off $z$, so $u$ is an articulation point. Now $x=r$ is an ancestor of $u$ and $y$ is a descendant of $u$, yet the path $r$-$y$ uses the back edge and misses $u$. (D) is false. Only (B) is correct.

shortcut.body: Recall the two textbook facts: the root is an articulation point iff it has at least 2 children, and a leaf never is. That settles (A), (B) and (C). For (D) one small graph (a triangle plus a pendant vertex) breaks the claim; 'all paths' is too strong when back edges exist.

traps.text: Believing the root can never be an articulation point. This is true only when it has one child; with two or more children, removing it separates the branches.
Thinking a leaf of $T$ can be an articulation point because a leaf of $G$ hangs by one edge. Removing a leaf never disconnects anything: the rest of the tree still spans the remaining vertices.

Believing every descendant is cut off from every ancestor by an articulation point $u$. Only the subtrees of $u$ that have no back edge above $u$ are cut off; a descendant with a back edge past $u$ stays connected.

recognize.clues: The stem defines an articulation point and refers to a DFS tree, its root, a leaf and ancestor/descendant pairs, which points to the root/leaf rules and the back-edge reasoning.
recognize.contrast: A bridge is the edge analogue and looks similar, but here the claims concern removing vertices, so the child-subtree and back-edge tests for vertices apply.

check.body: Test the root rule on the path a-b-c. Start the search at b: it visits a, then returns and visits c, so b has two children and removing b separates a from c. Start at a instead: the root has one child and removing a leaves b-c connected. The rule matches both runs.

questions.stem: Let $G=(V, E)$ be a weighted undirected graph and let $T$ be a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of $G$ maintained using adjacency lists. Suppose a new weighted edge $(u, v) \in V \times V$ is added to $G$. The worst case time complexity of determining if $T$ is still an MST of the resultant graph is

solutionDiagram.alt: A spanning tree with root r and a new dashed edge u-v of weight 5; the bold tree path u, a, r, b, v with weights 3, 7, 4, 2 shows the heaviest edge a-r of weight 7 exceeds 5.

steps.title: Terms and the cycle rule
steps.body: A minimum spanning tree (MST) $T$ connects all $|V|$ vertices with $|V|-1$ edges of least total weight. If you add an edge $e=(u,v)$ of weight $w$ to $T$, you get exactly one cycle: $e$ plus the tree path from $u$ to $v$. The cycle property says the heaviest edge of a cycle is not needed in an MST. So $T$ is still an MST of the new graph if and only if $w$ is at least the weight of the heaviest edge on that tree path; if $w$ is smaller, swapping that heavy edge for $e$ gives a lighter spanning tree.

steps.title: The algorithm and its cost
steps.body: Walk $T$ from $u$ with a DFS until you reach $v$, remembering the largest weight seen on the path, then compare it with $w$. The walk looks only at tree edges, and $T$ has $|V|-1$ of them, stored in adjacency lists, so the walk visits at most $|V|-1$ edges, which is $\Theta(|V|)$ in the worst case (a path-shaped tree where $u$ and $v$ are at opposite ends). The $|E|$ edges of $G$ are never touched, so $|E|$ does not appear. In the picture the tree path $u,a,r,b,v$ has weights 3, 7, 4, 2 and the new edge weighs 5; the heaviest tree edge, 7, exceeds 5, so swapping it for the new edge gives a lighter tree and $T$ is no longer an MST.

steps.title: Why the others are not the answer
steps.body: Checking $\Theta(|E|+|V|)$ would be the cost of searching the whole graph rather than only the tree. $\Theta(|E||V|)$ and $\Theta(|E|\log|V|)$ are the costs of recomputing the MST from scratch with a naive method or with Kruskal, which is unnecessary here. The tree-path test is correct and the cheapest, so the answer is (D), $\Theta(|V|)$.

shortcut.body: Adding an edge to a tree makes one cycle, and finding a path in a tree with $|V|-1$ edges is linear in $|V|$. An answer that mentions $|E|$ means recomputing the MST or scanning the whole graph, which is not needed. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(|E|+|V|)$ because a DFS on a graph costs that. The DFS here runs on the tree $T$ only, which has $|V|-1$ edges.
Choosing $\Theta(|E||V|)$ from a nested loop over edges and vertices. Nothing in the check needs a nested loop.
Choosing $\Theta(|E|\log|V|)$ by re-running Kruskal's algorithm on the new graph. That works but is the slow route.

recognize.clues: A tree T is already given, a single new edge is added, and the question asks only to decide whether T is still minimum, with an adjacency-list cost, so no rebuilding is needed.
recognize.contrast: Recomputing the tree with Kruskal or Prim also answers the question but costs far more; the cycle property shortcut only looks at the one cycle.

check.body: Check the lower bound with a path-shaped tree on $|V|$ vertices where the new edge joins the two ends. The cycle has $|V|$ edges and all must be inspected to find the heaviest, so no method can beat linear time in $|V|$. The cost does not grow with $|E|$, because non-tree edges are never touched.

questions.stem:
Let $G=(V, E)$ be a directed, weighted graph with weight function $w: E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. For some function $f: V \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, for each edge $(u, v) \in E$, define $w^{\prime}(u, v)$ as $w(u, v)+f(u)-f(v)$.

Which one of the options completes the following sentence so that it is TRUE?

"The shortest paths in $G$ under $w$ are shortest paths under $w^{\prime}$ too, ____".
options: if and only if $\forall u \in V, f(u)$ is positive
if and only if $\forall u \in V, f(u)$ is negative
if and only if $f(u)$ is the distance from $s$ to $u$ in the graph obtained by adding a new vertex $s$ to $G$ and edges of zero weight from $s$ to every vertex of $G$

steps.title: Terms and the question
steps.body: A path is a sequence of edges $v_0\to v_1\to\dots\to v_k$, and its weight is the sum of its edge weights. A shortest path from $s$ to $t$ is a path whose weight is smallest among all paths from $s$ to $t$. The question changes every edge weight by $f(u)-f(v)$, where $f$ gives each vertex a number, and asks when the shortest paths stay the same. The rule to test: if the change to the weight of a whole path depends only on its two ends, then it moves all paths with the same ends by the same amount and cannot reorder them.

steps.title: Add up the change along a path
steps.body: For the path $P=v_0\to v_1\to\dots\to v_k$,

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: Every term $f(v_1),\dots,f(v_{k-1})$ cancels in pairs (one added, one subtracted), so only $f(v_0)-f(v_k)$ remains. For all paths from $s$ to $t$ that shift is the same constant $f(s)-f(t)$. So the path of least $w$-weight is also the path of least $w'$-weight, whatever $f$ is, positive, negative, or mixed. A cycle has $v_0=v_k$, so its weight does not change either, and negative cycles stay negative. The sentence is true 'for every $f$': (A). A script confirmed on 2000 random graphs and random $f$ that the shortest-path sets are identical under $w$ and $w'$.

shortcut.body: Telescoping: the $f$ terms cancel inside a path and leave $f(\text{start})-f(\text{end})$, a constant per vertex pair. So any $f$ works and (A) is right. Options with 'if and only if' are suspicious, because the choice of $f$ in (D) is only what Johnson's algorithm picks to make weights non-negative.

traps.text: Choosing (D) because it describes Johnson's algorithm, which sets $f$ to the distance from a new source to make all new weights non-negative. That is a good choice for $f$, but it is not required for the shortest paths to be preserved.
Choosing (B) because positive numbers sound safe. The sign of $f$ plays no role, since only the differences $f(u)-f(v)$ enter and they telescope.
Choosing (C) for the same reason as (B): negative values of $f$ change nothing about which path is shortest.

questions.stem: Consider a graph $G=(V, E)$, where $V=\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_{100}\}$, $E=\{(v_i, v_j) \mid 1 \leq i<j \leq 100\}$, and weight of the edge $(v_i, v_j)$ is $|i-j|$. The weight of minimum spanning tree of $G$ is ____.

solutionDiagram.alt: Path v1, v2, v3 up to v99, v100 with every edge of weight 1, and a dashed edge from v1 to v3 of weight 2 that is not needed.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A spanning tree of a graph with 100 vertices connects them all with no cycle, so it has exactly $100-1=99$ edges. A minimum spanning tree (MST) has the smallest possible total weight. Here every pair of vertices is joined (a complete graph) and the edge $(v_i,v_j)$ has weight $|i-j|$, the distance between the indices. Rule: if each of the 99 edges has weight at least $m$, the total is at least $99m$, and if you can build a spanning tree reaching $99m$, it is minimum.

steps.title: Lower bound and a tree that meets it
steps.body: Every edge has weight $|i-j|\ge1$, since $i\ne j$ are integers. A spanning tree has 99 edges, so its weight is at least $99\cdot1=99$. Now take the 99 edges $(v_i,v_{i+1})$ for $i=1,\dots,99$, each of weight 1. They form the path $v_1,v_2,\dots,v_{100}$: connected, no cycle, 99 edges, a spanning tree of weight 99. It meets the lower bound, so it is an MST. (Kruskal's method does the same: it takes all 99 weight-1 edges first, and they already connect everything.)

shortcut.body: Any spanning tree has 99 edges and every edge costs at least 1, so the answer is at least 99; the path $v_1v_2\dots v_{100}$ achieves it. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: 100: using the number of vertices instead of edges. A tree on 100 vertices has 99 edges.
4950: adding every edge weight of the complete graph or counting its $\binom{100}{2}$ edges. The MST uses only 99 of them.
98: stopping at 98 edges by an off-by-one, or counting the unit gaps between $v_2$ and $v_{100}$ only.

recognize.clues: A complete graph with a simple closed-form weight $|i-j|$ and a request for the minimum spanning tree weight, which Kruskal solves by taking the cheapest edges first.
recognize.contrast: Prim would give the same weight, but for such structured weights a counting bound (edges times least cost) is quicker than running either algorithm.

check.body: Use a second route: an exchange argument. Any spanning tree that contains an edge of weight 2 or more has 99 edges, so its total is at least $98\cdot1+2=100$, which is above 99. Only trees made entirely of weight-1 edges can reach 99, and the path $v_1v_2\dots v_{100}$ is one.

questions.stem:
Let $G$ be any connected, weighted, undirected graph.

I. $G$ has a unique minimum spanning tree, if no two edges of $G$ have the same weight.

II. $G$ has a unique minimum spanning tree, if, for every cut of $G$, there is a unique minimum-weight edge crossing the cut.

Which of the above two statements is/are TRUE?

steps.title: Terms and the cut rule
steps.body: A spanning tree connects all vertices with no cycle; a minimum spanning tree (MST) is one of least total weight. A cut splits the vertices into two non-empty sides $S$ and $V\setminus S$, and an edge crosses the cut if its ends lie on different sides. The deciding rule (cut property): if an edge $e$ is the only lightest edge crossing some cut, then every MST contains $e$. Reason: if an MST $T$ lacked $e$, then $T+e$ has a cycle, and that cycle crosses the cut a second time at some edge $f\ne e$ with $w(f)>w(e)$; swapping $f$ for $e$ gives a lighter tree, which contradicts that $T$ is minimum.

steps.title: Statement II is true
steps.body: Take an MST $T_1$ and any edge $g$ of it. Removing $g$ splits $T_1$ into two parts, which is a cut, and $g$ is the only edge of $T_1$ crossing it. By the assumption this cut has a unique lightest edge, and by the cut rule every MST contains it, so $T_1$ contains it, so it must be $g$. Hence every edge of $T_1$ is the unique lightest edge of some cut and lies in every MST. Any other MST $T_2$ therefore contains all $|V|-1$ edges of $T_1$, so $T_2=T_1$.

steps.title: Statement I is true
steps.body: If no two edges have the same weight, then in every cut the lightest crossing edge cannot be tied with another, so every cut has a unique lightest edge. That is exactly the hypothesis of II, so the MST is unique. Both statements are true: (C). A script confirmed on random 5-vertex graphs, by counting all minimum spanning trees by brute force, that the count is 1 under each hypothesis.

shortcut.body: Statement I is a special case of II: distinct weights force a unique lightest edge across every cut. So if II is true, I is true; and II is the standard sufficient condition for a unique MST. Both true. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Accepting I but rejecting II because II sounds less familiar. II is the more general condition and is also sufficient.
Accepting II but rejecting I because distinct weights seem too weak. Distinct weights imply II, so I is true as well.
Believing an MST can be non-unique even with distinct weights. Ties between equal weights are the only source of several MSTs.

recognize.clues: Both statements say a spanning tree is unique under a condition on weights or on cuts. The words 'for every cut' and 'unique minimum-weight edge crossing the cut' name the cut property directly.
recognize.contrast: Kruskal and Prim only build one tree; they do not decide uniqueness. Uniqueness is a property question, settled by the cut property and ties, not by running an algorithm.

check.body: Take a triangle with weights 1, 2, 3. Every cut has a unique lightest crossing edge and all weights differ. The only candidate trees are the three pairs of edges, with totals 3, 4 and 5, so exactly one tree has the least total. Now give two edges the same weight and a second tree of equal total appears, which shows ties are the only way to lose uniqueness.
