questions.stem:
Let $G$ be a simple undirected graph. Let $T_D$ be a depth first search tree of $G$. Let $T_B$ be a breadth first search tree of $G$. Consider the following statements.

(I) No edge of $G$ is a cross edge with respect to $T_D$. (A cross edge in $G$ is between two nodes neither of which is an ancestor of the other in $T_D$.)

(II) For every edge $(u, v)$ of $G$, if $u$ is at depth $i$ and $v$ is at depth $j$ in $T_B$, then $|i-j|=1$.

Which of the statements above must necessarily be true?

solutionDiagram.alt: A triangle s, a, b. In the BFS tree a and b are both at depth 1 so edge a-b has depth difference 0. In the DFS tree s, a, b form a path and the dashed edge s-b joins an ancestor to a descendant.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: A depth first search (DFS) goes as deep as it can along one edge before backing up, and records a tree of the edges that discovered new vertices. A breadth first search (BFS) visits vertices layer by layer, so the depth of a vertex in $T_B$ is its edge-distance from the start. A cross edge joins two vertices where neither is an ancestor of the other in the tree. Test each statement: prove it for every graph, or find one graph where it fails.

steps.title: Statement I holds for undirected graphs
steps.body: Suppose edge $(u,v)$ exists and DFS reaches $u$ first. DFS does not finish $u$ until it has examined every edge at $u$, so $v$ is either already discovered (then it is an ancestor of $u$, since it is still active) or gets discovered during $u$'s visit, making it a descendant of $u$. In both cases $u$ and $v$ are ancestor and descendant, so an undirected DFS has no cross edges: I is true.

steps.title: Statement II fails on a triangle
steps.body: Take a triangle on $s,a,b$ and start BFS at $s$. Both $a$ and $b$ are neighbours of $s$, so both sit at depth 1. The edge $(a,b)$ then has $|1-1|=0\ne1$. BFS only guarantees that the depths of the two ends of an edge differ by at most 1, not exactly 1. So II is false and the answer is (A). A script on 3000 random connected graphs found 0 cross edges in the DFS trees and many edges with depth difference 0.

shortcut.body: Undirected DFS never makes cross edges (every non-tree edge is a back edge), so I is true. A triangle kills II, since two vertices at the same BFS depth can be adjacent. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing (B). It confuses BFS, where depths differ by 0 or 1, with an exact difference of 1. It also wrongly doubts the DFS fact.
Choosing (C) by assuming BFS depths of adjacent vertices always differ by one. Two neighbours of the same vertex are at equal depth and can be adjacent.
Choosing (D) because cross edges exist in directed DFS. In an undirected graph every non-tree edge links an ancestor and a descendant.

recognize.clues: The stem asks about cross edges in a DFS tree of an undirected graph and about depths of edge ends in a BFS tree. Both point at how the search order classifies edges.
recognize.contrast: Directed DFS does produce cross edges, so the fact that undirected DFS has none must not be carried over to directed graphs. BFS depths of an edge's ends differ by 0 or 1, never by exactly 1 in every case.

check.body: Run DFS on a triangle from one vertex: the DFS tree is a path, and the third edge joins the start to the vertex two levels down, an ancestor and descendant pair, so no cross edge appears. Run BFS on the same triangle: the two neighbours of the start both have depth 1 and are joined by an edge, so the depth difference is 0 and II fails.

questions.stem:
Consider the following undirected graph $G$:

Choose a value for $x$ that will maximize the number of minimum weight spanning trees (MWSTs) of $G$. The number of MWSTs of $G$ for this value of $x$ is ____.
questions.figure: Undirected graph on five vertices a, b, c, d, e. Edges with weights: a-b 4, a-c x, a-d 1, a-e 3, b-d 4, d-e 4, c-e 5. Vertex a is at the top, b at the left, c at the right, d at the bottom left and e at the bottom right.

diagram.alt: Undirected graph on five vertices a to e. Top a is joined to b (4), c (x), d (1) and e (3); b-d has 4, d-e has 4 and c-e has 5.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same graph with x set to 5. Edges a-d (1) and a-e (3) are bold as forced, a-b with b-d and a-c with c-e are medium pairs that each give two choices, and d-e is dashed as never used.

steps.title: Terms and the counting rule
steps.body: A spanning tree of 5 vertices has exactly 4 edges, connects every vertex and has no cycle. A minimum weight spanning tree (MWST) has the smallest total weight. Kruskal's method takes edges from lightest to heaviest and skips an edge that closes a cycle. Several MWSTs exist only when equal-weight edges are interchangeable, and then the count is the product, over each weight class, of the number of valid choices.

steps.title: The forced edges
steps.body: The edge $a$-$d$ (1) and $a$-$e$ (3) are the two lightest and make no cycle, so every MWST has them. Now $a$, $d$, $e$ form one piece and $b$, $c$ are single vertices. The edge $d$-$e$ (4) would close the cycle $a$-$d$-$e$, so it is never used.

steps.title: Attach $b$ and $c$
steps.body: Vertex $b$ can join only through $a$-$b$ (4) or $b$-$d$ (4): equal weight, so 2 choices. Vertex $c$ can join through $a$-$c$ (weight $x$) or $c$-$e$ (5). If $x\neq5$, the lighter one is forced and gives 1 choice. If $x=5$ the two tie and give 2 choices. So $x=5$ maximizes the count, and every MWST has weight $1+3+4+5=13$.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body: With $x=5$ the choices for $b$ and $c$ are independent: $2\times2=4$ MWSTs. A brute-force count over all 4-edge subsets gave 2 for every other tested $x$ (including $x=4$, where $a$-$c$ is forced) and 4 for $x=5$.

shortcut.body: Edges of weight 1 and 3 are forced and weight 4 on d-e is useless. Only b and c each have a tie to create, and x=5 is the only value that ties c; the answer is 2 x 2 = 4. About 1 minute.

traps.text: 2: choosing $x=4$ or another value and counting only the tie at $b$. At $x=4$, the edge $a$-$c$ is forced, so $c$ adds no choice.
3 or 6: counting $d$-$e$ as one more choice for $b$. It closes the cycle $a$-$d$-$e$, so it cannot be used.
13: giving the weight of the MWST instead of the number of them.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the number of minimum weight spanning trees and lets one weight vary. Counting trees with a free parameter points to ties among equal-weight edges in Kruskal's order.
recognize.contrast: Prim's method gives one tree from one run, and the MST cut property proves uniqueness. Here you are counting, so you treat each weight class and multiply the independent choices.

check.body: Check by total weight. With $x=5$ every MWST has the forced edges 1 and 3, one edge of 4 for $b$ and one edge of 5 for $c$, so each weighs $1+3+4+5=13$ and the choices at $b$ and $c$ are independent, giving 4. With $x=4$ the edge $a$-$c$ is cheaper than $c$-$e$, so the MWST weight drops to 12 and $c$ has one way to attach, leaving 2 trees.

questions.stem: The Breadth First Search (BFS) algorithm has been implemented using the queue data structure. Which one of the following is a possible order of visiting the nodes in the graph below?
questions.figure: Undirected graph on six vertices in two rows. Top row: M, N, O. Bottom row: R, Q, P. Edges: M-N, N-O, M-R, M-Q, N-Q, O-Q, O-P, Q-P.

diagram.alt: Undirected graph on M, N, O in the top row and R, Q, P in the bottom row, with eight edges: M-N, N-O, M-R, M-Q, N-Q, O-Q, O-P and Q-P.

solutionDiagram.alt: BFS layers from P: P at layer 0, O and Q at layer 1, N and M at layer 2, R at layer 3. The visit order is P, O, Q, N, M, R.

steps.title: Terms and the single rule
steps.body: Breadth First Search (BFS) uses a queue (first in, first out). Start at a vertex. Visit it, then put all its unvisited neighbours in the queue, in any order, then repeat with the vertex at the front. Rule: in a valid BFS order, right after the start vertex come all of its neighbours (in any order), then the new neighbours of the first of them, and so on. A vertex can appear only after a neighbour that was already taken from the queue.

steps.title: Neighbour lists
steps.body: M: N, R, Q. N: M, O, Q. O: N, Q, P. P: O, Q. Q: M, N, O, P. R: M.

steps.title: Test each option, one start at a time
steps.body: (A) MNOPQR starts at M, whose neighbours N, R, Q must be the next three vertices. The third vertex is O, which is not a neighbour of M. Invalid. (B) NQMPOR starts at N, whose neighbours M, O, Q must come next. The fourth vertex is P, which is not a neighbour of N. Invalid. (C) QMNROP starts at Q, whose neighbours M, N, O, P must be next. The fourth vertex is R, which is not a neighbour of Q. Invalid.

steps.title: Check (D)
steps.body: POQNMR starts at P: its neighbours O and Q come next, in that order, as required. O is first in the queue, and its only new neighbour is N, so N is next. Q's only new neighbour is M, so M is next. N brings nothing new. M brings R. The order is P, O, Q, N, M, R, which matches (D). A script that simulates the queue confirmed that only (D) is possible.

shortcut.body: For each option, take its first vertex and check that the vertices right after it are all neighbours of it, and that nothing non-adjacent jumps in early. A, B and C fail within three letters. About 40 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing MNOPQR because the letters are in alphabetical order. BFS must list all of M's neighbours before any vertex two edges away, and O is two edges from M.
Choosing NQMPOR because N, Q, M are all neighbours. Then P, two edges from N, appears before the neighbour O.
Choosing QMNROP because the first three are neighbours of Q. R is two edges from Q but is placed before the neighbour O.

recognize.clues: The stem says BFS is implemented with a queue and asks which visiting order is possible. A 'possible order' question means checking each option against the layer-by-layer rule.
recognize.contrast: DFS orders may dive to a distant vertex straight after the start. An order that jumps two edges away before finishing the start's neighbours can only come from DFS, not from BFS.

check.body: Use a second route, distance from the start. In any BFS order the distances from the first vertex never decrease. From P the distances are O 1, Q 1, N 2, M 2, R 3, so POQNMR reads 0,1,1,2,2,3 and passes. Option B, starting at N, lists P (distance 2) while the neighbour O (distance 1) is still unvisited, so it breaks that rule.

questions.stem:
Let $G=(V, E)$ be any connected undirected edge-weighted graph. The weights of the edges in $E$ are positive and distinct. Consider the following statements:

(I) Minimum Spanning Tree of $G$ is always unique.

(II) Shortest path between any two vertices of $G$ is always unique.

Which of the above statements is/are necessarily true?

solutionDiagram.alt: A 4-cycle a, b, d, c with weights a-b 1, a-c 2, c-d 3, b-d 4. The three lightest edges in bold are the unique MST. Both paths a-b-d and a-c-d from a to d weigh 5, so the shortest path is not unique.

steps.title: Terms and the two claims
steps.body: A minimum spanning tree (MST) connects all vertices with least total edge weight and no cycle. A shortest path between two vertices is a path of least total weight. 'Distinct' means no two edges share a weight. Test each claim: prove it, or find one graph that breaks it.

steps.title: Claim I is true
steps.body: Suppose two different MSTs $T_1$ and $T_2$ exist. Among the edges in one tree but not the other, pick the lightest, $e$, say $e\in T_1$. Adding $e$ to $T_2$ makes a cycle, and that cycle has some edge $f\notin T_1$ (since $T_1$ has no cycle). Then $f\in T_2\setminus T_1$, so $w(f)>w(e)$ by the choice of $e$ and by distinct weights. Swapping $f$ for $e$ gives a spanning tree lighter than $T_2$, contradicting that $T_2$ is minimum. So the MST is unique.

steps.title: Claim II fails
steps.body: A shortest path adds up weights, and different sums of distinct numbers can still be equal. Take a 4-cycle $a,b,d,c$ with $w(a,b)=1$, $w(b,d)=4$, $w(a,c)=2$, $w(c,d)=3$: all positive and distinct. From $a$ to $d$, the path through $b$ costs $1+4=5$ and the path through $c$ costs $2+3=5$, so there are two shortest paths. Hence only (I) is necessarily true: (A). A script on random graphs with distinct weights found exactly one MST every time.

shortcut.body: Distinct edge weights make the MST unique, but sums of weights along paths can tie. Only I is true. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Choosing (B) by believing distinct weights make path sums distinct. Sums of different edges can be equal, as 1+4 and 2+3.
Choosing (C) by extending the uniqueness of the MST to shortest paths. Uniqueness comes from comparing single edges, not sums.
Choosing (D) after finding that II fails, without checking I. I holds for every graph with distinct weights.

recognize.clues: The weights are positive and distinct, and the question asks what is necessarily unique. Distinct weights are the standard sufficient condition for a unique MST, while path uniqueness is a different property.
recognize.contrast: Shortest paths add weights along a route, so distinct edge weights do not make path lengths distinct. Dijkstra's tie-breaking can return either of two equal shortest paths.

check.body: On the four-cycle with weights 1, 2, 3, 4 arranged as $1,4$ on one route and $2,3$ on the other, both routes between opposite corners total 5, so two shortest paths exist while the weights stay distinct. The same graph has the unique MST made of the edges 1, 2 and 3, so the two claims separate.

hints.text: The two statements ask about different things: one tree for the whole graph, and one path for each pair of vertices. Decide for each whether it can fail even though all weights differ.
Recall the exchange argument for minimum spanning trees: take an edge in one tree but not the other, add it to the other tree, and look at the cycle that forms.

Ask what each statement has to compare. One compares single edge weights against each other; the other compares totals over several edges. Check whether distinct single weights control each kind of comparison.
To test statement II, look for a small graph with two routes between the same two vertices that use different edges but add to the same total.
Draw a four-cycle and list the two routes between a pair of opposite corners. Each route uses two edges, so try to share the four weights out between the routes.

variation.stem: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected undirected graph with positive, distinct edge weights. (I) The heaviest edge of $G$ is never in a minimum spanning tree of $G$. (II) For adjacent vertices $u,v$, the edge $(u,v)$ is always the shortest path from $u$ to $v$. Which of the statements is/are necessarily true?
variation.explanation: If the heaviest edge is a bridge, every spanning tree must use it, so I fails: take edges $ab=1$, $bc=2$, $ac=5$, $cd=9$. In the same graph the edge $ac$ weighs 5 but the path $a,b,c$ weighs 3, so II fails as well. Neither statement is necessarily true.
